title: Past participles and present perfect with har
goal: Recognize the past-participle forms needed for har + past participle and use Norwegian present perfect for present-relevant meaning.

objectives.statement: Recognize the past-participle forms needed for har + past participle and use Norwegian present perfect for present-relevant meaning.

sections.title: A new flat, but not everything is ready

spans.value: Maja has recently moved into a new flat. Her friend Sander arrives shortly before Maja’s parents are due to visit.
Har du pakket ut alt?
Jeg har pakket ut klærne, men jeg har ikke åpnet eskene med bøker.

blocks.translation: I have unpacked the clothes, but I haven’t opened the boxes of books.

spans.value: Har du funnet kaffetrakteren?

blocks.translation: Have you found the coffee maker?

spans.value: Ja, men jeg har glemt å kjøpe kaffe.

blocks.translation: Yes, but I have forgotten to buy coffee.

spans.value: Det går bra. Jeg har kjøpt kaffe og brød på veien.

blocks.translation: That’s all right. I have bought coffee and bread on the way.

spans.value: Perfekt. Foreldrene mine kommer snart, og jeg har ikke ryddet kjøkkenet.

blocks.translation: Perfect. My parents are coming soon, and I haven’t tidied the kitchen.

spans.value: Jeg har allerede vasket benken. Nå tar vi eskene sammen.

blocks.translation: I have already cleaned the counter. Now we’ll deal with the boxes together.

spans.value: The conversation is about actions in the past, but the speakers care about their results now. The clothes are out of their boxes, the books are still packed, and there is now coffee for the visitors. This connection between a past action and the present is the central meaning of the Norwegian present perfect.
The present perfect (presens perfektum) consists of two parts:
har + past participle (perfektum partisipp)
Har is the present-tense form of å ha, to have. The past participle is a special form of the main verb.
The whole expression is used for completed actions or experiences connected to now, and for situations that began earlier and continue now. Har does not change according to the subject:
The past participle also stays the same in this construction:
A common mistake is to change har when the subject changes. Norwegian does not use different forms corresponding to English has and have.
Incorrect:
Correct:

Many past participles are easy to recognize once you have met the verb’s main forms. However, there is no single ending that works for every Norwegian verb. Learn the past participle as part of the verb.
Some common verbs have participles ending in -et:
Other common verbs have shorter participles:
Several frequent verbs have forms that must be learned individually:
The infinitive ending alone does not always tell you the participle. For example, å kjøpe becomes kjøpt, not ✗ kjøpet, and å skrive becomes skrevet, not ✗ skrivet.
When a dictionary gives forms such as kjøpe – kjøpte – kjøpt, the final form, kjøpt, is the one used after har.

The present perfect connects earlier time with the present. In the patterns taught here, it presents completed actions or experiences connected to now, or situations that began earlier and still continue. It often answers a practical question such as: What is ready now? What has happened so far? What experience does someone have now?

sections.title: A completed action with a result now

spans.value: Maja says:
The unpacking happened earlier. Its result matters now: the clothes are no longer packed.
Compare:
The important result is that they have coffee now.
The loss happened earlier, but the current problem is that the speaker does not have the key.
The dinner is ready now.
The action does not need to have happened only a few minutes ago. What matters is the present connection.

no.value: Jeg har lest boka, så du kan låne den.

en.value: I have read the book, so you can borrow it.

no.value: De har solgt bilen og tar bussen nå.

en.value: They have sold the car and take the bus now.

spans.value: The present perfect can also describe experience within a period that reaches the present.

no.value: Jeg har vært i Bergen tre ganger.

en.value: I have been to Bergen three times.
She has never seen the northern lights.
Have you eaten Norwegian brown cheese?

spans.value: The exact occasion is not the point. The speaker is asking or stating what belongs to someone’s experience up to now.
Words such as allerede, already, aldri, never, and ennå, yet, often fit this meaning:

en.value: We have already seen the film.

no.value: Jeg har aldri prøvd dette før.

en.value: I have never tried this before.

spans.value: These words do not create the present perfect. They help show how the past event is viewed from the present.

sections.title: A situation that began earlier and still continues

spans.value: Norwegian also uses the present perfect for a situation that started in the past and is still true now.

no.value: Jeg har bodd her i to år.

en.value: I have lived here for two years.
We have known each other for a long time.

no.value: Hun har jobbet på hotellet siden mai.

en.value: She has worked at the hotel since May.

spans.value: The time expressions support the present connection:

items.value: i to år means for two years: a length of time.
siden mai means since May: a starting point.

spans.value: The situation has not been presented as finished. Jeg har bodd her i to år normally means that I still live here.
A likely mistake is to use only the present tense because the situation is still true. Norwegian uses har + past participle when the speaker includes the period from the past up to now.
Incorrect for the intended meaning:

no.value: ✗ Jeg bor her i to år.

en.value: I live here for two years.

spans.value: Correct:

no.value: Jeg har bodd her i to år.

en.value: I have lived here for two years.

sections.title: Present relevance versus a finished past occasion

spans.value: The present perfect normally does not locate an event at a specific, finished past time such as yesterday or last year. If the speaker reports what happened during a finished past occasion, Norwegian generally uses the past tense (preteritum).
Compare the viewpoints:

no.value: Så du den filmen på fredag?

en.value: Did you see that film on Friday?

no.value: Hun har vært i Tromsø mange ganger.

en.value: She has been to Tromsø many times.

no.value: Hun var i Tromsø i fjor.

en.value: She was in Tromsø last year.

spans.value: The coffee is available now. No finished past time is specified.
The speaker places the event yesterday.
This asks about experience up to now.
This asks about a particular finished occasion.
The visits belong to her experience up to now.
The visit is located in a finished year.

This chapter does not require you to produce all past-tense forms. The contrast helps you make the present-perfect choice: use har + past participle when the past event is viewed through its result, experience, or continuation now.
A common error is to combine the present perfect with a finished-time expression:
Incorrect in ordinary use:

no.value: ✗ Jeg har kjøpt boka i går.

en.value: I have bought the book yesterday.

spans.value: For present relevance, remove the finished time:
If yesterday is the point, the sentence needs the past-time viewpoint:
The central verb form remains har + past participle in statements, negatives, and questions.

en.value: I have not opened the box.

spans.value: Do not replace the participle with the infinitive after har.
Incorrect:
Incorrect:
Correct:
A little later, Maja’s parents arrive.
Så fint det har blitt her!

blocks.translation: It has become so nice here!

spans.value: Takk! Vi har åpnet nesten alle eskene.

blocks.translation: Thanks! We have opened almost all the boxes.

spans.value: Og vi har ryddet kjøkkenet.

blocks.translation: And we have tidied the kitchen.

spans.value: Har dere spist?
Nei, vi har ikke spist ennå.
Da passer det bra. Jeg har laget suppe.

blocks.translation: Then that works well. I have made soup.

spans.value: The forms now do practical work in the conversation. Maja reports what is ready, Kari asks about the situation now, and the soup she made earlier is relevant because everyone can eat it now.

sections.title: Transfer: preparing for a weekend trip

spans.value: Now change the situation. Amir and Nora are leaving for a cabin this afternoon. They need to check what is ready before they go.
Relevant statements might include:

no.value: De har ikke kjøpt mat ennå.

en.value: They have not bought food yet.

no.value: Amir har vært på hytta før.

en.value: Amir has been to the cabin before.

spans.value: The same construction now serves several closely related present-relevant purposes: completed preparations with results now, something still not done, and relevant experience.

prompt.value: Read the statements and choose the interpretation that explains why the present perfect is useful now.

options.text: Det viktigste er bare en ferdig fortid, uten forbindelse til nå. (The only important point is a finished past, without a connection to now.)
options.why: The lesson presents these statements through their present results.

options.text: Nøkkelen er borte nå, middagen er klar nå, og boka kan lånes nå. (The key is unavailable now, dinner is ready now, and the book can be borrowed now.)
options.why: The present results are the reason for choosing the present perfect.

prompt.value: A speaker asks about experience at any time up to now, not about one particular finished occasion. Which sentence fits?

options.text: Så du den filmen på fredag? (Did you see that film on Friday?)
options.why: The finished occasion is located on Friday.

options.text: Hun var i Tromsø i fjor. (She was in Tromsø last year.)
options.why: The finished occasion is located in last year.

options.text: Har du spist norsk brunost? (Have you eaten Norwegian brown cheese?)
options.why: The question asks whether the experience has happened at any time up to now.

prompt.value: Classify the four situations and choose when har plus a past participle is appropriate.

options.text: A og C har forbindelse med nå og bruker har + partisipp; B og D gjelder ferdige fortider. (A and C connect to now and use har + past participle; B and D concern finished past occasions.)
options.why: A reports a current result and C asks about experience; B and D specify finished past occasions.

options.text: Alle fire bruker har + partisipp. (All four use har + past participle.)
options.why: B and D locate events in finished past times.

options.text: Bare B og D bruker har + partisipp. (Only B and D use har + past participle.)
options.why: B and D are the finished-time contrasts, not the present-relevant cases.
